text: Several complementary, non-chemical methods reduce weed damage in rice, and combining them works better than relying on any single one. Hand weeding (pulling weeds out by hand) remains a widely used and effective method, though it is labor- and time-intensive. Mechanical weeding with a push-type rotary weeder between rows is generally more efficient than hand weeding for larger areas, but requires some skill to use without damaging rice roots, and the field should be drained of standing water before using this tool so the weeder can grip and uproot weeds properly. Water management is one of the cheapest and most effective tools: maintaining a standing water depth of about 5-10 cm effectively suppresses broadleaf and sedge weeds, though grassy weeds are more water-tolerant and may still need combined control even under flooding. Good land leveling also matters because it lets water spread evenly across the field; on an uneven field, high spots that stay dry become footholds where weeds establish and spread even if the rest of the field is flooded. Planting density affects weed pressure directly: closer spacing (for example around 10x10 cm) closes the rice canopy faster and shades out weeds much more effectively than wider spacing (such as 20x20 cm), which leaves more open ground and light for weeds to exploit -- so a properly dense, even stand is itself a form of weed control. Where these cultural methods are not enough, herbicides can be used (see the separate herbicide selection entry in this knowledge base for how to choose and apply them appropriately).
